title: Foundation Medicine Adult Cancer Clinical Dataset (FM-AD)
summary:
The Foundation Medicine Adult Cancer Clinical Dataset is the largest single cohort in the Genomic Data Commons: 18,004 patients across many tumor types, profiled with a targeted DNA panel in a clinical rather than research setting. That scale is genuinely useful for questions about mutation frequency and co-occurrence in a real-world population, which is precisely where research cohorts are least representative.
It is also the clearest case in this corpus of a dataset whose catalog entry invites analyses it cannot support. Vital status is populated for 100% of cases and informative for 0% - every value is "not reported". Race is "not reported" for all 18,004 patients. Every treatment field is empty. Progression and last known disease status are populated for every case and informative for none. A researcher attracted by the sample size will find, after obtaining controlled access to 54,012 files, that no outcome-anchored analysis is possible.
one_liner: 18,004 patients profiled with a targeted clinical panel - the largest cohort in the Genomic Data Commons, with no informative vital status, no race data, and no treatment records.

useful_for.question: What are the mutation frequencies and co-occurrence patterns of clinically targeted genes in a large real-world oncology population?
useful_for.rationale: 18,004 patients profiled on a clinical panel give tight confidence intervals on alteration frequencies, including for alterations too rare to study in a thousand-patient research cohort. Frequency and co-occurrence need only the variant calls and the tumor type, both of which are present.
useful_for.statistical_note: Panel composition bounds what can be counted: absence of a gene from the panel is not absence of alteration. Report frequencies only for genes on the panel and state the panel version.

evidence.note: Written by a named reviewer after reading the source documentation and the measured field coverage. Not machine-generated.

useful_for.question: How does the mutational landscape of clinically sequenced patients differ from that of research cohorts such as TCGA?
useful_for.rationale: Clinical sequencing populations are enriched for advanced and pretreated disease relative to the largely treatment-naive primary tumors in research cohorts. With 18,004 cases the comparison is well powered, and the discrepancy is itself a caution about generalising research-cohort findings to clinical practice.
useful_for.statistical_note: Restrict the comparison to genes present on both assays and to matched tumor types; differences in assay sensitivity and tumor purity confound naive comparisons.

useful_for.question: How common are actionable alterations across tumor types in routine practice?
useful_for.rationale: Scale plus a clinically-deployed panel makes this the right cohort for estimating what fraction of patients would be eligible for a given targeted therapy, a question that research cohorts systematically answer wrong.
useful_for.statistical_note: Eligibility estimates apply to the population that received clinical sequencing, which is not the whole cancer population.

limitations.statement: Vital status is populated for 100% of the 18,004 cases and informative for 0%: every value is "not reported". Progression or recurrence and last known disease status show the same pattern - fully populated, entirely uninformative. No outcome endpoint of any kind can be derived.
limitations.mitigation: None. Choose a different cohort for any outcome question.

limitations.statement: Every treatment field is empty for every case: prior treatment, treatment type, therapeutic agents, treatment outcome and line of therapy are all at 0% coverage.
limitations.mitigation: None. Note that this is a clinically sequenced and therefore largely pretreated population, so alteration frequencies reflect an unrecorded treatment history.

limitations.statement: Race is recorded as "not reported" for all 18,004 patients. The largest cohort the Genomic Data Commons holds contributes nothing to any question about how cancer genomics differs across populations.
limitations.mitigation: Germline-based ancestry inference is not appropriate here; the assay is a tumor-only targeted panel and the consent scope does not contemplate it.
